description: We’re building Earth Pulse, a platform that uses NASA satellite data and local records to explore heat, vegetation, air quality, and urban growth in Cochabamba, Bolivia. We work with geospatial analysis, data science, web/mobile development, and AR/VR. We’re looking for teammates interested in GIS, machine learning, environmental science, and UX/UI. Join us to turn Earth observation data into clear, interactive tools for local communities.
summary: Earth Pulse turns satellite observations and local records into an interactive environmental atlas of Cochabamba, Bolivia. We developed a web platform, an Android app with augmented reality, and a Meta Quest virtual reality experience to explore heat, vegetation, air quality, and urban growth across the city's 15 districts. NASA/USGS Landsat, NASA MODIS, and NASA POWER data are combined with municipal geography, monitoring stations, and other public datasets. Users can compare districts, inspect historical series, examine trend significance, and export results. An exploratory greening simulator shows the estimated association between increased vegetation and surface temperature, including uncertainty. By connecting Earth observations with familiar places and accessible visualizations, Earth Pulse addresses the Earth System Trend Detective challenge and helps residents, students, researchers, and municipal teams investigate environmental change and discuss better-informed urban planning.
details:
Earth Pulse helps people investigate how their city is changing by connecting satellite observations with local environmental and urban records. Developed around Cochabamba, Bolivia, the platform brings together information about its 15 districts in a shared experience across the web, Android, augmented reality, and Meta Quest virtual reality.

Our data pipeline processes NASA/USGS Landsat surface temperature and reflectance, NASA MODIS temperature, vegetation, and annual land cover, and NASA POWER meteorological variables. These datasets are combined with municipal buildings, zoning, transportation, public facilities, local air-quality records, airport weather observations, and university field measurements. Python scripts handle quality filtering, geographic processing, temporal aggregation, and the generation of reusable datasets served through a FastAPI backend.

The explorer provides 15 thematic layers covering surface temperature, vegetation, elevation, urban development, infrastructure, monitoring locations, environmental trends, and estimated PM10. Users can select and compare districts, inspect values and historical charts, filter observations, and export CSV files. Comparing planned land use with observed land cover also helps users investigate how urban development relates to the municipal plan.

Trend analysis uses Theil–Sen slopes, Mann–Kendall testing with an autocorrelation adjustment, and multiple-testing correction. Results retain information about significance, uncertainty, and data availability. A gradient-boosting model reconstructs historical PM10 using monitoring records, meteorology, and urban context. Its district estimates remain exploratory because the available monitoring network provides limited spatial validation.

The “What if?” greening simulator explores surface-temperature differences associated with changes in vegetation. It presents uncertainty and applicability information, helping users understand the assumptions behind each scenario. The model describes an observed association between vegetation and surface temperature; establishing the effects of a real intervention requires further investigation.

Our creative contribution is making the same environmental evidence available through several ways of exploring a city. The responsive web and mobile interfaces support everyday access. The Android AR experience places a three-dimensional atlas on a detected surface, while the Quest application presents an interactive city model with spatial panels and comparison tools.

We used Python, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, Shapely, scikit-learn, and FastAPI for processing and analysis; React, TypeScript, MapLibre, and Recharts for the interface; Capacitor, Three.js, Java, and Google ARCore for Android; and Unity, C#, and Meta XR for VR.

Throughout development, we considered readability, touch interaction, device performance, source attribution, missing observations, differing spatial resolutions, and scientific uncertainty. The interface distinguishes surface temperature from air temperature and observations from modeled estimates. Our intended impact is to strengthen environmental education, community participation, and informed discussion about urban planning.
